newsitem.title: THAILAND: IMF seen overtaking central bank role in Thailand.
newsitem.headline: IMF seen overtaking central bank role in Thailand.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is expected to override Thailand's central bank and call the shots in running the country's ailing economy during the coming months, analysts said on Tuesday.

They said the successor to outgoing governor Rerngchai Marakanond would have his job shaped mostly by monetary and fiscal disciplines that would be imposed by the IMF in the aftermath of Thailand's de facto devaluation of the baht.
On Tuesday the Thai cabinet appointed deputy central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi as the new governor.
Thailand confirmed on Monday that it was seeking IMF advice to put its economy back on an even keel and could possibly seek a credit line from the world body.
That decision overshadowed any impact that would normally arise from a change of its central bank governor, analysts said. The Thai stock market and baht firmed sharply despite the news.

"It makes no difference who will be Rerngchai's successor in term of policy. I would say for the next six months, the new governor would not have much choice but to walk the IMF line. His job would be made easier," said Kitti Limsakul, economics lecturer at Chulalongkorn University.
Few analysts were surprised by Rerngchai's resignation.
They said the former governor had previously hinted he may quit. He was also perceived as being closely associated with ex-Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan in resisting a baht devaluation.
Amnuay quit in June partly over policy conflicts with other cabinet ministers. Thailand let the baht float on July 2 and it has lost nearly 20 percent of its value since.
"His resignation is a product of changing circumstances," Kitti said.

Warut Siwasariyanon, head of research at Ing Baring International Pte Ltd said: "Rerngchai is generally seen in the no-devaluation camp. He and Amnuay focused on maintaining baht stability. After Amnuay left, he looked helpless trying to stop the tide of letting the baht float."
Warut said Rerngchai had not formulated central bank policies alone and Chaiyawat would carry on the practice while preserving the Bank of Thailand's relative independence.
He said an IMF austerity package being adopted by Thailand should include tough measures of improving the current account and balance of payments.

Kitti of Chulalongkorn University said that with Rerngchai and Amnuay gone, the pressure on shoring up the battered economy would rest on Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh and his new Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya.
"Chavalit could not keep passing the buck. If the economy failed to show signs of bottoming out soon, the prime minister would also have to take the heat, politically," he said.

The economist said Chavalit and politicians in his six-party coalition would need to display a spirit of helping the country by agreeing to additional serious budget cuts which would likely be recommended by the IMF.

"It would be good if the defence, education, interior and communications ministries agreed to another 60 billion baht in budget cuts. Chavalit needs to show his political courage and his political allies need to sacrifice," Kitti said.
Thailand's economic turmoil would contribute to its first, and heavy, government budget deficits in 10 years this year and in 1997/1998 (October-September) fiscal year.

Before his departure Amnuay pushed through the cabinet a 26 billion baht ($839 million) cut from the 1997/1998 budget. Opposition politicians said another 50-60 billion baht in expenditure must be trimmed from next year's planned spending.
"It remains to be seen how willing politicians would be in complying with the IMF when it comes to giving up budgets," Kitti said.
